study.title: Genesis 39 - Joseph in the house of Potiphar and in prison
study.overview: The chapter shows the contrast between Joseph's faithfulness and the injustice he suffers. Even as a slave and then as a prisoner, the Lord is with him, gives favor to the eyes of others and makes his work prosper. At the same time, the text highlights Joseph's integrity in the face of sexual temptation, his refusal to sin against God and the way in which false accusation leads him to prison without erasing the providential presence of God in his life.

outline.title: José thrives in the house of Potiphar
outline.explanation: Joseph is bought by Potiphar, and although he is in a condition of bondage, the Lord accompanies him. The presence of God becomes visible in the success of his work, in the trust of the lord and in the blessing that reaches the whole house of the Egyptian because of him.

outline.title: Temptation, resistance and false accusation
outline.explanation: Potiphar's wife tries to seduce Joseph repeatedly, but he firmly refuses, calling upon the trust of his lord and the fear of God. When she falsely accuses him, Joseph loses his clothes, his reputation and his freedom, being cast into prison by the wrath of Potiphar.

outline.title: The Lord is with Joseph in prison
outline.explanation: Even in prison, the Lord continues with Joseph, gives him mercy and favor, and puts him in a position of responsibility. The chapter concludes by reaffirming that Joseph's prosperity did not depend on the place, but on the presence of the Lord with him.

study.context: The chapter resumes Joseph's story after his sale to Egypt. The notes highlight the contrast between Joseph's integrity in Potiphar and Judah's moral failure in the previous chapter. They also note that Potiphar was a Pharaoh's officer and captain of the guard, linked to the king's administration and the royal prison. The mention that the prisonhouse was linked to the prisoners of the king helps to understand why Joseph's arrest was not a total abandonment, but an environment where God's providence continued acting.
study.theology: The text emphasizes God's active providence in adverse circumstances. The recurring expression that the Lord was with Joseph shows that divine favor is not annulled by slavery, injustice or imprisonment. Joseph is also an example of moral fidelity: he rejects sin not only by human allegeness, but because sinning against Potiphar's wife would be to sin against God. There is also a theme of mediated blessing: because of Joseph, the Egyptian house is blessed. Thus, the narrative unites personal holiness, unjust suffering and advancement of divine purpose. Matthew Henry's notes also observe a figure of Christ in Joseph, but this should be read as a typological interpretation, not as a direct statement of the chapter.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter presents Joseph as someone in whom the Lord was, making him prosperous and also a blessing, despite his slavery and after the arrest.
Joseph resists his lady's temptation and refuses sin with awareness that this would be wickedness against God, not just against men.
Even in prison, the Lord continued with Joseph and granted him great favor in the guinea pigger's eyes, showing that his prosperity depended on the presence of God.

questions: What does the repetition that the Lord was with Joseph teaches about the presence of God in stages of humiliation and injustice?
Why does Joseph present his refusal as sin against God, and not just as an offense against men?
How does Joseph's prosperity, both in the house of Potiphar and in prison, redefines what success is before God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the believer to unite fidelity and trust. In practice, this means maintaining integrity when no one is seeing, rejecting temptations even when they are persistent and interpret difficult circumstances in the light of God's presence, not just the immediate outcome. It also encourages to serve diligently where one is, trusting that the Lord can use common work, suffered injustice, and improbable places to fulfill his purposes.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are selective and do not comment each verse in detail; therefore, some links between the scenes were summarized from the flow of the chapter itself. Joseph's typological reading as a figure of Christ appears in Matthew Henry and should be understood as devotional interpretation, not as an explicit conclusion of the text. There is not enough base in the notes to safely state more historical details about the prison beyond what is mentioned.
